processing: Steamed green tea made as sencha and upper-grade sencha, also roasted into hojicha.
harvest_season: Spring first flush is the most valued, as with other Japanese sencha; high gardens generally run later than lowland ones.
appearance_dry: Dark green sencha needles, as is usual for the class.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green, typical of mountain sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf pieces, like other sencha.
taste_profile: Few detailed tasting notes exist; as with other high mountain sencha, expect clean fragrance and a fresh, lightly brisk finish.

brewing.notes: Standard sencha method. Hojicha from the same growers takes boiling water and a short steep.

vintage_note: Sold in the current year's sencha and upper sencha, plus hojicha, tea bags and bottled drinks. It often appears under the brand name Shimanto Headwaters tea, so look for both names. As usual for green tea, drink it fresh.
description:
Tsunoyama-cha is the tea of Tsuno town in western Kochi, grown across five districts of the town. Today much of it is sold under a second name, Shimanto Headwaters tea, which tells you where it is: the headwaters of the Shimanto.

The range is the familiar one: sencha and upper sencha plus hojicha.

Little has been written on how it tastes. Treat it as mountain sencha, brew it cool, and judge the fragrance over the first two steeps.

It is rarely seen outside Japan, so look for it through hometown-tax or producer channels and check the harvest year.
history:
Tea from these districts is said to have been among Kochi's representative teas from the Edo period; details of who began it and how it developed are thinly documented.

The Shimanto Headwaters branding is the name most buyers now see.
